review:
Prior to this, we had very few good games based on movie/comics characters (only Chronicles of Riddick and Spudi man 1-2 from the top of my mind), so even with positive previews from press, it was really hard to believe that rather inexperience studio will give us anything decent.

But oh boy they delivered. It has very good pace to it, so balanced that the game ends right at the point when you start to get bored.
It has very generous difficulty progression, so if you never played any other game with this style kick+counter+dodge combat (in which, for the full credit, Batman AA was rather innovative at the time), you won't feel like the game throws at you a riddle impossible to solve.
It has decent story its not as elaborate as yours masses of effects or planescapes torments, but it does the job and keeps at least me invested into throughout 8 hour campaign. Although if you are not into comics stuff, it won't be easy to follow, because most of the game is basically a fan service, including iconic animated batman voice cast.

One of the few negatives this game has - its upgrade system. Half of the Batman gear's upgrades are optional, and another half are simply unnecessary, and used only to get all the Riddler's challenges.

Overall if you haven't played this game and just want to try Arkham series out, it is a valid option to do so, however I'd suggest to skip it and jump straight into Arkham City, which is the complete Batman Arkham experience. At this point Arkham Asylum in my opinion is worth to buy and play only in case if you've completed AC and AK and want more quality content.

[b]There are great superhero games, and then there is Batman: Arkham Asylum, a game so breathtakingly awesome that it redefined the superhero genre. This 2009 masterpiece is not just a Batman game; it’s a love letter to the Dark Knight, Gotham’s villains, and the entire Batman universe.[/b]

[h1]A Dark, Gritty Masterpiece[/h1]
[b]From the moment you step into Arkham Asylum, you feel the chilling atmosphere of Gotham’s most notorious prison. The story pulls you in right from the start, trapping you inside with Joker, Harley Quinn, Bane, Killer Croc, Scarecrow, and more. Every hallway, every cell, and every shadow is filled with tension, making you feel like you’re one step away from disaster at all times.[/b]

[h1]Gameplay: The Batman Experience[/h1]
[b]This game perfectly captures what it feels like to be Batman. The combat system is smooth, satisfying, and brutally cinematic. The stealth mechanics make you feel like a true predator, stalking criminals from the shadows. And let’s not forget the detective mode, which brings out Batman’s genius side, solving puzzles and hunting down secrets like a true detective.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Masterpiece of storytelling: Every moment is gripping, dark, and engaging.
[*]Fluid and innovative combat system: The Freeflow Combat system revolutionized action games.
[*]Incredible voice acting: Mark Hamill’s Joker and Kevin Conroy’s Batman are perfection.
[*]Atmospheric world design: Arkham Asylum feels alive, terrifying, and full of mystery.
[*]Stealth mechanics: Feel like a true shadow in the night, taking down enemies one by one.
[*]Detective elements: Showcases Batman’s intelligence, not just his strength.
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Some boss fights feel a bit repetitive: But they still capture the essence of Batman’s villains.
[*]Limited open world: Unlike later Arkham games, this one is more confined (but still amazing).
[/list]
[h1]Conclusion: A Timeless Classic[/h1]
[b]Batman: Arkham Asylum is the true masterpiece of 2009, a game that set the gold standard for superhero games and continues to inspire the genre. It’s a dark, gripping, and unforgettable experience, proving that WB and Rocksteady created something legendary.
If you love Batman, if you love action games, or if you just love masterfully crafted stories, this game is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED.[/b]

This game is a dream come true for Batman fans. It hits that classic, mysterious Batman which is cold, calculated, experienced, and always focused. The graphics still hold up today, and the atmosphere is incredible. Some areas even managed to scare me, which says a lot due to the enemy design, sound design and overall mood of the game.
There are plenty of villains to face and many areas to explore. The map feels tight and focused, but the Asylum's courtyard and buildings are filled with secrets, unlockables, and challenges. The combat is smooth and satisfying, it's not overly complicated. It's very fun, especially on hard difficulty.

The art style is fantastic. You can tell this was made in a time when developers cared about every detail, even the main menu. Browsing through it feels satisfying.
The story delivers, and the unlockables add a surprising amount of depth to the villains. You actually want to read about them which is rare. Discovering the island's history through old relics and recordings adds another layer to the experience. 
The cutscenes, voice acting, and overall tone are entertaining, dark, and sometimes even unsettling. 
Not everyone will walk out of Arkham Asylum unscathed.
The attention to detail is everywhere. As you progress, Batman grows a bit of a beard, his suit gets damaged, his cape tears, and he starts to look bruised and worn down. It keeps you immersed from start to finish.

The only weak point is the final boss fight...it's a bit of a letdown and mostly just waves of enemies. 
But honestly, the rest of the game is so strong that it barely matters.
This is still one of the best superhero games ever made: rich story, great atmosphere, amazing voice acting, smooth gameplay, and tons of content to unlock.

I replayed the whole Arkham series once again in the beginning of this year and this review was due so here I go! Without Batman: Arkham Asylum, we wouldn't have gotten any of the Insomniac's Spider-Man games. That is the LEGACY which this game carries. Even years after release, Batman: Arkham Asylum still feels like the moment superhero games finally grew up. Before this, most superhero titles were decent at best, forgettable at worst. Rocksteady changed that completely.

It introduced [b]Freeflow[/b] combat system. Even after 16 years, it feels incredibly satisfying. Punches feel heavy, counters flow smoothly, and when you build a long combo it genuinely feels like you’re Batman dismantling a room full of thugs. Stealth sections, Perching on gargoyles, the Detective Mode, gadgets, and level design make these encounters replayable and creative.

Overall this is the weakest of the Arkham games overall, boss fights are easily the weakest part, often relying on repetitive Titan enemy encounters instead of unique villain battles. Customization is also basically nonexistent but it is a master in [b]atmosphere[/b]. The comic-book style and gothic nature of Arkham Asylum is what sets it apart from the other Arkham games, and if you're planning to play them, don't skip this one just for being the clunky original. Unfortunately, the game does suffer from being the first in-terms of gameplay as it can feel very clunky to play, but the story and aforementioned style carries it towards still being a great game. 

Despite a few dated elements, Batman: Arkham Asylum remains one of the most atmospheric superhero games ever made. It might not have the scale of its sequels, but it absolutely nailed the feeling of being Batman and the horror of Arkham Asylum.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is still one of the best superhero games ever made, even years after its release. From the moment you step into Arkham, the atmosphere pulls you in—dark, gritty, and perfectly capturing the essence of Gotham’s most infamous asylum.
The combat system is smooth and incredibly satisfying. The “free-flow” mechanics make you feel like Batman himself, chaining punches, counters, and takedowns effortlessly once you get the rhythm. It’s easy to learn but rewarding to master.
What really stands out is the attention to detail. The story is engaging, with strong voice acting (Mark Hamill’s Joker is unforgettable), and the characters feel true to the comics. Each villain encounter feels unique and memorable.
Exploration is another highlight. The asylum is packed with secrets, Riddler trophies, and hidden lore that reward curiosity. Using Batman’s gadgets and detective mode adds variety to both combat and puzzles.
That said, the game is a bit linear compared to later entries in the series, but it works in its favor by keeping the experience tight and focused.
Overall, Batman: Arkham Asylum is a must-play, especially if you enjoy action-adventure games or are a fan of Batman. It set the standard for superhero games and still holds up remarkably well.

This is a great game. The fighting and the vibe are so good that you can easily look past the parts that feel a little old.

The story is solid for a superhero game, but what really stood out were the collectibles. Instead of just picking things up, many of them are riddles where you have to find a specific object in the area. It’s way more engaging, and totally doable without a guide. The fact that there’s even a built-in map tracking all of them is pretty crazy for a 2009 game. It felt really satisfying to 100% the game without constantly alt-tabbing to a YouTube video.

Combat on hard is where the game really shines. It plays like a rhythm game: you have to time your hits to keep the combo flowing. Button mashing resets your combo, which means no special moves and fights drag out. There’s a learning curve, but once it clicks, it’s amazing. Batman starts flying around the room taking dudes out without missing a beat. My only complaint is that some gadgets don’t feel that impactful. You mostly use them just to keep the combo going.

Stealth is okay for a 2009 game, but a little clunky. Takedowns and gliding feel restrictive, and you can’t even make noise(without a late-game gadget) to lure goons. Bosses are pretty meh too. Some turn into platforming sections where you’re just running and dodging, and others are big brawls with waves of enemies. Nothing really stuck with me. The music is fine but not particularly memorable.

There aren’t a ton of enemy types, but the game is short enough that it never drags. The length feels perfect: you finish it and feel satisfied, or you immediately want more.

Even years later, Arkham Asylum is still a blast to play. The combat and atmosphere make it easy to forgive a few clunky bits, so I highly recommend it.

Back in 2009, when I first played Arkham Asylum as a kid with my little brother, it felt like stepping into Batman’s mind. The dark atmosphere, that haunting menu music, the gritty hallways of the asylum—it all left a mark on us. We’d take turns sneaking through vents and beating up thugs, completely hooked. It wasn’t just a game, it was an experience. Every shadow felt alive, every encounter intense. We didn’t even realize how much this game was shaping our love for Batman.

Now playing it again, that same darkness still creeps in. The twisted vibes, the tension in every corner, and Kevin Conroy’s legendary voice still give me chills. It’s not just a great game, it’s a time capsule of pure emotion and childhood memories. RIP Kevin Conroy. You were the voice of our hero, and your legacy lives on in every line.

Coming back to Batman: Arkham Asylum 16 years later shows just how ahead of its time it really was. The gameplay still feels distinct, and the overall experience easily holds its own against many modern titles.

The progression system is satisfying. Unlocking new gadgets, upgrading combat, and using Detective Mode to track enemies or clues gives a strong sense of control without ever becoming overwhelming. Everything fits naturally into Batman’s world.

The world-building stands out as well. Riddler trophies, character bios, and interview tapes add meaningful layers to the story. It never feels like filler, just thoughtful details that deepen your connection to Arkham and its characters.

The boss fights are unique and well-designed, with each one offering a challenge that fits the villain’s personality. The voice acting is still top-tier. Every character feels fully realized, and the performances bring the story and tone to life without forcing it.

Most impressively, the creativity behind Arkham itself is what makes the game truly timeless. The gothic architecture, eerie atmosphere, and layered lore turn the asylum into more than just a backdrop. It’s a fully realized world with history, tension, and identity. Every hallway and hidden room feels intentional, packed with details that reward exploration and reinforce the game’s Gotham roots.

Rating: 9/10 – A creative, well-crafted experience that’s stood the test of time and remains a benchmark for superhero games.

Today 10 years ago, Batman finally got the videogame he deserved. I can't believe it has been this long since I first played this game. I expected some average superhero game that, with a bit of luck, was somewhere on the same level as the Batman Begins game. If someone would have told me this game would somewhat define modern action adventures, I would have called them crazy. This game truely caught everyone by surprise and in many ways, this still is the best arkham game if you ask me.

That dark atmosphere of the asylum remains untouched, the soundtrack does its part perfectly to enhance that feeling, the combat starts out as button mashing but evolves into something really special that might be easy to learn, but is hard to master. Voice acting is on point due to the classic voices you might know from the animated series and the overall gameplay loop just is a great mix of combat (freeflow + predator), puzzle solving and exploration. Well, and even the graphics hold up surprisingly well 10 years later.

Still, no game is perfect, and when it comes to this game... the boss battles really are not that good. Fighting Bane the first time is awesome, but prepare yourself for the same fight multiple times throughout the game. There is Killer Croc that is pretty cool, but not really a boss fight, the Scarecrow sections are really good, but those are the exceptions. Fighting Poison Ivy is simply done by dodging her attacks and spamming quick batarangs and I won't even mention that final fight.

Anyway, those flaws can hardly bring down the rest of the game, that honestly seemed like perfection back in the day... untill Arkham City came out 2 years later and improved on pretty much everything gameplay wise. To conclude this, if you haven't played this game as a fan of action adventures and/or Batman, you should really do that. And if you plan on playing the whole series I highly recommend starting out with this one. Coming back after playing the sequels, the gameplay can seem like a downgrade, so make sure you play in order of release. Thanks to everyone who read this whole thing, have a nice day and be the Batman!

Well, for starters, this game was a blast back in 2010-2011. Everyone talked about it, everyone was praising Rocksteady Studios for how precisely they showed us the best of Batman's comic universe, with that prominent Tim Burton's Special, a good mixture of darkness, tragedy, and grotesque, which feels like a proper seasoned blended scotch...

We should also mention a brilliant 'easy to learn, hard to master' battle gameplay which was then copied by the dozens if not hundreds of different games, combined with one of the best stealth gameplay experiences. Plus a good portion of exploring and puzzle-solving - again, one of the best implementations of that notorious collectibles hunting, heavily spiced with so many Gotham's lore as possible.

If you're a fan of Batman universe, you probably already know and love this game. And even if you're not a fan of Batman, you may like the depth, the overall endeavor of this fine example of how the developer should use its AAA budget to make a really good game overall. I mean, for the year 2010, it was all top-notch: the visuals, the sound work (especially the voicing, with all those sound distortion effects, and famous actors playing the main roles), gameplay, the whole comic series lore application... Sadly, that spark of true involvement and striving to make the best possible game was later killed by the same developers and even bigger budgets. The latest Batman Arkham games are known as quite mediocre ones, mostly because of the technical issues, and the lack of creativity.

So, speaking of the whole Rocksteady Batman Arkham series, Arkham Asylum is probably the best one, in terms of game development. The most balanced one, the most thought-over. But at the same time, the most outdated one. Visuals are still great, but... For example, the overextended main hero figure surely was planned to be just like that in this all-too-complex-wrap-of-the-game. But, by modern standards for third-view action games, the scale of characters on the screen is just... to big to be comfortable. The figure of Batman is simply obscuring almost a third of any frame in the game, except stealth sequences. That's getting really inconvenient in the exploring, and not really all that much helping in the fighting.

Also, you've probably noted the alcohol reference at the beginning of this review. I've used it with more purpose than just a simple attempt to explain the taste of the story. You see, the ESRB rating for this game is 'TEEN', and technically, it's almost correct. Sex and drugs references, as well as the extreme violence, are all there, but - again, technically - they are mild. Mild. As with the mild sorts of cigarettes, that still kill you - but doing it gently. Kinda. The same goes with the main clutch of the whole story, where Joker plays his master plan, killing and hurting hundreds of people, to get in touch with Batman. In that hypertrophied analogy with teenagers who are trying to prove something - to themselves, to the world, to their parents - by doing absolutely wild, desperate, and just stupid things. In the short version, on the paper, it all sounds good enough for the 'Teens' rating. But, that darkness... that grotesque... In my humble opinion, it goes a bit over the head for the most bunch of modern world teens. My own kids are almost at that 'teens' age, and I'm certain that the story of Arkham Asylum, even when covered with all that 'mild' camouflage, still not fitting them even a bit. Maybe 16+... In some cases, even 18+ people would really take a hint of what's going in the game. Like, actually feel it. And yet it's way too grim. Try to watch Edward Scissorhands movie with some 12 y.o. sometime? Yeah, exactly that kind of grotesque.

Well, maybe if you're not a self-aware and compassionate type, and just play the games to beat some bad guys, it's not a real matter for you. Then again, maybe Arkham Asylum will not fit you simply because there are not as many fights as you might be expecting. 

The point that I'm trying to explain is about some controversies in the game - in all of the major parts. Fighting feels a bit off thanks to the giant character figures that partially obscures the view, and also exactly because of that glorious 'freeflow' battle system, which ain't really that much freeflow. Some of the Batman's moves, combined with the partial screen obscureness, simply break those 'freeflow'-chained combos. And it feels like you're trying to play some basic melody on the piano, say [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=prfOc0r-CSQ]Chopstiks[/url] for example - and losing tempo every time. And then like 'okay, let's start this over'... Again, and again... It's not really hard to beat all the game, even with all those combo-breaking things. Just a perfectionist itch. All the game is not that hard as achieving the 'freeflow', using all the Batman moves in a line.

The same pattern goes with exploring. Generally, it's cool: some lore elements are hidden across the Arkham island, and you can collect them to affix yourself to the Batman world (and get some exp point to develop some Batman tools in the process). Or you can ignore those collectibles, and simply move through the story events. A cool idea, and generally well-implemented... except the thing that some tools you'll need for exploring, will be unlocked much later in the game. It is making the backtracking issue much more severe, and hey, guys who love the exploring part, tell me, how much do you love to return to previous locations to use some new tool and get to some previously locked place? Lovely, isn't it?

With all that said, Batman Arkham Asylum is still a great game. Just too dark to recommend it to my son, yet. And kinda tedious for those players who can't take this game as a whole, and look only for some adventure, or some skull-crushing, or hide-and-seek playtime... Also, Batman himself isn't that much the great 'superhero', being a very tedious and detached figure, who enjoys too much running in circles, for such a proposedly smart guy. But maybe it's just me outgrowing comic book stories.

The overall mark is 8/10. It is a very good game. Just not for everyone.

This is an extended review on Batman: Arkham Asylum.

Content: 9/10
A 10+ hours campaign story along with a great challenge mode, which also has DLC challenges included, that can extend the length of the game up to 30 hours or even more in some cases. Unlockable character bios which include character interviews that you can listen to and character trophies, all of which are rewarded to you for your play time or geekness for searching and finding the Riddler's trophies. Very nice. Worth mentioning is that the game features a "Game +" which can extend the game's play value and play time by a lot more. (for those who are daring enough to endure the harder combat and lots of deaths that will follow)

Graphics: 9/10
Except from the eventual low res textures, which are hidden very well that in some cases are not even noticeable, the game looks amazing even to this day when maxed out. And this is a console port, which shows that the developers gave the time and effort to make it look as good as it could on a powerful enough machine.

Aesthetics: 10/10
This game catches the nitty gritty and dark enviroment, in which the Dark Knight fights villains for the good of Gotham. The Arkham Asylum really feels like a psychiatric prison that went wrong!  Not much more can be said.

Sound: 9/10
- Sound Quality: It is excelent, crisp and clean as it should be in any game.
- Soundtrack: Be it on scenes, menus, combat or non-combat it fits the spirit of the game and that's what matters. It is great, it feel like soundtrack for a Batman licenced product.
- Lip synching: While it is really good it feels like it could be better. One of the better lip synching i have seen in a game though.

PC Port: 9/10
- Display Settings: From Anti-Aliasing, Dynamic Shadows and Distortion to Harmonic Lighting, Ambient Occlusion and PhysX, this game has a lot of settings that will satisfy the PC enthusiants just fine. (Although the FOV slider is missing. I know, its not a FPS game but still, its not there. you can mess with the files though and set it to your liking)
- Controls: This game supports controllers and rebindable keys which is a god send! Only 2 problems, 1 minor, 1 big. 1) You cannot rebind your keys while in-game, you have to do it before you launch the game via the game launcher and, 2) As many console to PC ported games tend to do, there are actions, many of them in fact, that are binded to a single key and that can cause some problems and a lot of frustration. Be aware.
- Optimization: This game has been tested and completed using an Nvidia GeForce GTX 570 Sonic Edition. With Motion blur being turned off (cause my eyes hate it) and Bloom being turned off (cause apparently my card hates it), this game was being maxed out on 1080p 60 fps (with V-Sync turned on). Greatly optimized in my opinion.

Story: 10/10
You are Batman, escorting the Joker, an unpredictable and very dangerous villain to a psychiatric high security hospital-prison called the "Arkham Asylum", where he escapes, and its up to you to stop him, the prison break he just caused and the other "super-villains" that are lurking free in the asylum.

Gameplay: 9/10
While simplistic in its design, Batman: Arkham Asylum's gameplay is so good and successful that it already has spawned a mechanical clone (namely the Middle Earth: Shadow of Mordor game) and probably many more will follow. 
- Combat: The combat in theory is an action beat-them-up with counter moves and special moves that can be executed when you have reached a big enough combo on the press of a button, but it is so much more in praticality, making the game the opposite of a chore. Satisfaction is the word that can describe it. And of course you can make Batman learn new moves and combos while leveling up, making the combat even better while you progress through the game.
- Non-Combat: When there are no enemies to fight, the game includes a lot of puzzles to solve (the Riddler's trophies) but most of them are no big deal (key word being "most" of them). Use the batclaw to traverse through the island or just use your feet!
- Present in both combat and non-combat is the dedective mode, which helps you solve riddles or progress the storyline in some cases in non-combat and helps you indentify the weakness of special enemies or super-villain encounters/bosses in combat. Also, the Bat-gadgets, like for example the iconic Batarang or the Batclaw, these tools are there to help you battle enemies, traverse through the island or solve Riddler's puzzles. You unlock new gadgets while progressing through the game.
Although i will mention that combat has its hic-ups. There are times that Batman wont counter when you press the button or wont target the correct enemy or even wont hit an enemy because he isnt close enough when that isnt the case. There is room for improvement here.


To conclude, Batman: Arkham Asylum is a shining example of how a Batman game or generally a superhero game is ought to be. Full of great content, amazing story and satisfying gameplay, this is a game that you are doing yourself a disservice if you actually havent purchased and played it yet. Full price or on a Steam Sale this game is worth your buck.

The critically acclaimed Batman: Arkham Asylum defines what a Batman game, and to a larger extent, a superhero game should be. It begins with Batman arriving at the infamous Arkham Asylum, a psychiatric hospital that houses the most dangerous and clinically insane inmates in Gotham City. Among them is, of course, the Joker. Soon enough the Joker has escaped and takes control of the asylum while releasing all the other criminals in the process. We must then navigate the dark and atmospheric asylum, from its cramped gloomy halls to its open outdoor areas replete with gothic facades, using Batman's superior detective skills to find clues and carry the narrative forward. Along the way we come across many notable characters, as well as some of Batman's most fearsome rivals.  Batman's portrayal in this game is both iconic and layered, voiced by Kevin Conroy. Likewise, the Joker, voiced by Mark Hamill, is a constant thorn in Batman's side and is the perfect rendition for this game. 

Visually, this game was far ahead of its time and remains impressive to this day. Environments are rich, with great lighting effects and textures. With the views of Gotham City in the distance, the sense of isolation is foreboding. The character models are beautifully detailed and represent the quintessential look of these classic heroes and villains. The game has a high sound quality design, greatly adding to the immersive experience. Sound effects are spot on, and the music ebbs and flows with the pacing and arrival or departure from certain areas. The aformentioned voice acting is another highlight, with stellar performances for all the major leads. 

The fluid and dynamic free-flow combat system is intuitive but also complex. Combat is very rewarding and Batman can chain combos with various moves and counters as well as integrate his gadgets. Taking on a room full of thugs and laying them all out is so satisfying. The combat challenges will really put your skills to the test, and completing them all will require advanced proficiency of this combat system. Batman can also deal with situations through stealth mechanics, allowing him to strike from the shadows, hang off various objects and take down enemies one by one as they frantically try to figure out what is happening. 

Arkham Asylum is the blueprint for future Batman sequels and sets the bar high for subsequent superhero games. The story, character representations, visuals, sound, and gameplay are all top notch. I can repeatedly return to this game and consider it a must play for those that have yet to do so.

[h1]Batman: Arkham Asylum: A Near-Perfect Batman Game[/h1]

[h2]TL;DR[/h2]

Batman: Arkham Asylum barely feels its age where it matters. The combat is simple but satisfying, predator encounters make you feel genuinely dangerous, Arkham Island is packed with atmosphere and secrets, and the voice acting and art direction still hold up remarkably well.

Its biggest weaknesses are repetitive boss fights, Detective Mode being almost too useful, and a few mechanics the sequels would eventually refine.

[b]9.5/10: An exceptional Batman game that still deserves to be played.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Combat & Predator Gameplay[/h2]

Arkham Asylum's FreeFlow combat is deceptively simple. Attacking, countering, stunning, evading, and using gadgets is easy to understand, but maintaining long combos while responding correctly to different enemies gives the system much more depth.

Once you find the rhythm, Batman effortlessly moves between enemies and a well-executed fight can look almost choreographed. Later games expanded the system considerably, but the foundation here is already excellent.

[b]The predator encounters might be even better.[/b]

Against armed enemies, you stalk guards from gargoyles, hide beneath floor grates, create distractions, use gadgets, and quietly remove them one at a time. Watching the survivors become increasingly terrified remains incredibly satisfying.

My main complaint is Detective Mode. Seeing enemies through walls and highlighting important objects is extremely useful, but it is [i]so[/i] useful that there is often little reason to turn it off. For a game with such excellent environments, spending so much time looking through a blue filter is unfortunate.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Arkham Island & Exploration[/h2]

[b]Arkham itself might be the best part of the entire game.[/b]

Rather than giving Batman a huge open world, Rocksteady confines the game to a relatively small interconnected island. Medical facilities, botanical gardens, caves, cell blocks, and abandoned sections all feel distinct while still belonging to the same place.

New gadgets gradually open previously inaccessible paths, giving exploration a light Metroidvania structure. Returning to older areas stays worthwhile because there is usually a Riddler trophy, interview tape, riddle, or hidden area you could not reach earlier.

The Riddler challenges are especially good because many require you to actually observe the environment rather than simply follow icons on a map.

[b]Arkham Asylum proves that a smaller, carefully designed world can be more memorable than a massive one filled with filler.[/b]

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Story, Villains & Atmosphere[/h2]

The setup is simple: Batman delivers Joker to Arkham, Joker takes control of the asylum, and one terrible night begins.

The plot itself is not particularly complicated, but its strength comes from the characters, atmosphere, and constant feeling that Joker is controlling everything around you.

Kevin Conroy is excellent as Batman, while Mark Hamill completely owns the role of Joker. His constant taunting over the asylum's PA system keeps him present even when you have not physically seen him for a long time.

Scarecrow is another standout. His sequences are among the game's most memorable moments because they completely change the atmosphere and start messing with the rules you have become accustomed to.

Unfortunately, [b]the boss fights are probably Arkham Asylum's weakest element.[/b] Several rely on repetitive attack patterns rather than properly testing the combat and predator mechanics, and the final confrontation does not live up to the buildup.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Progression & Presentation[/h2]

Progression is straightforward but effective. Experience unlocks new combat techniques, armor upgrades, and gadget improvements, while new equipment gradually expands both combat and exploration.

Visually, the technology obviously comes from the late 2000s, but [b]the art direction has aged far better than the raw graphics[/b]. Gothic architecture, industrial interiors, heavy shadows, rain, grime, and increasingly damaged environments give Arkham a fantastic identity.

The audio is equally strong. Combat sounds brutal, enemies panic during predator encounters, and the soundtrack complements the atmosphere without overwhelming it.

The PC version is old enough that legacy features such as PhysX can occasionally require extra attention on modern hardware, but the game itself remains extremely lightweight.

[hr][/hr]

[h2]Final Thoughts[/h2]

Batman: Arkham Asylum is smaller and mechanically simpler than its sequels, but its focus is one of its greatest strengths.

The bosses could have been better, Detective Mode is overpowered, and later games refined nearly every individual system. Yet Arkham Asylum remains special because everything works together so well.

If you like Batman, this is an easy recommendation. Even if you do not, it remains an excellent action game that helped establish a combat and stealth formula countless games would later borrow from.

[b]More than anything, Arkham Asylum understands Batman: the fighting, detective work, intimidation, gadgets, villains, atmosphere, and feeling of being one person walking into a building full of criminals who gradually realize they should be afraid of you.[/b]

[b]9.5/10: Nearly perfect. Absolutely recommended.[/b]

As you can clearly observe from my profile, I've literally "completed" the game and obtained all the unlockable achievements. As such, I found it sensible to share my  personal review of the cult classic above and express the genuine admiration I feel towards it.
Additionally, I've also "platinumed" the remastered version of the game on PS4 so I will draw some small comparisons for those indecisive about the primary platform they prefer to experience the masterpiece on.
Also, this'll probably turn out to be a fairly long and discursive discourse so proceed at your own discretion.

[b] Personal Attachment [/b] :
Before I delve into an actual "review" of the product, I'd like to elaborate a bit on the special place it occupies in the depths of both my memory, and heart:
It was 2009.
The 9 year old me had only just finally convinced my hard-going father to buy me an XBOX 360 as a reward for my then outstanding elementary school performance (Just your typical Asian family stuff). Upon the purchase of the console, as I was inspecting the store shelves, scanning the innumerable glowing cases of green which I was yet to own a sample of, my eyes drifted toward the portrait of a familiar tenebrous character that stood out menacingly among all the other present promotional artworks.
It was the same caped crusader I grew up watching a highly praised animated show of;
the very same "Dark Knight" I'd watched a recent Hollywood adaptation of;
It was the ultimate embodiment of [i] vengeance [/i]
It was a veiled creature of the [i] night [/i]
That is correct, it was [i] BATMAN [/i] !

Spare me the cringe.

Regardless, I instantly knew I'd decided upon the game I was gonna pick for my then new console.
A decision which ultimately booked me an exclusive ticket to the sumptuous festival that was to be held at the notorious mad clown's renovated amusement park: the [i] Arkham Asylum [/i] !
And boy if it didn't turn out to be a hell of a roller coaster ride.

Admittedly though, upon my first attempt at the title, I failed to play it to completion. Perhaps the mechanics were a tad too sophisticated for the [i] minor [/i] me and my frail understanding of the English language didn't exactly help with my progression (FYI English is not my primary language, so incidentally, pardon any possible errors that may occur in my composition).
Regardless, I dropped the game and didn't pick it back up until shortly after the release of Arkham City. Having grown at least a few years older, with improved knowledge around the "foreign language", I decided to give the first entry another go and consequently, finished it for the first time before jumping to the highly acclaimed sequel.

A few years later, a console-exclusive remaster of the first two classics was announced to be hitting the shelves. Of course, being the avid “Gothamite” that I am, there was no hesitation on my part to purchase, play and "Platinum" the game on my PS4.
When I finally converted to the "PC master race" and came across a generous discount of the game during the steam holiday sale, I couldn't fight the urge to buy, play and complete the game once again. Which brings me to the next point:

[b] TECHNICAL ASPECTS (WITH COMPARISONS) [/b] :
The PC experience, despite the slightly muddier textures and somewhat lower-resolution cutscenes, easily manages to hold its own against the fully remastered variants.
The [i]con[/i] -sole versions are capped at 30 fps (unless you insert the unpatched physical disc into a 9th gen console), a limitation which imposes a significant hindrance on the overall fluidity of the gameplay.
These remasters are also mostly recognizable for employing a sharper, more vibrant color tone which in my humble opinion takes away from the intended dark, eerie atmosphere of the game and the asylum. The only departments in which the console alternatives maintain an upper hand are clearer textures, 1080p cutscenes (which are still pre-rendered with a noticeably low bitrate) and the addition of precipitation. And admittedly, the rain effect truly does make the outdoor environment of the game look a whole generation apart from the classics.
But with the addition of multiple modification packs available for the game on PC, notably Asylum Reborn, along with 4K upscaled cutscenes that are downloadable separately, the 13 year old PC version of the title is beyond capable at delivering a satisfactory visual performance.

[b] NARRATIVE EXPERIENCE [/b]
This is probably one of the rare instances in which the game doesn't seem to utilize its full potential. The story doesn't exactly offer anything too deep or emotionally engaging and instead presents you with the usual, ever-recurrent, Tom & Jerry-esque trope of "Batman chasing Joker to stop his sinister scheme". But the mere atmosphere of the asylum, the detail and attention put into the making of it and the pure thrill and joy that is derived from exploring it, more than make up for the cliché plot that's still relatively fun to follow.
The small yet boisterous selection of the rogue gallery who are admitted to the asylum, each get their own tumultuous time to shine and a renowned few who don’t make the cut are cleverly referenced or alluded to -invoking speculations on future possibilities.
Not to disregard the single ingredient that truly brings out the long-lasting flavor of this palette-numbing haute cuisine: the invaluable inclusion of the holy trinity of all non-live-action Batman media: Arleen Sorkin, Mark Hamill and the late Kevin Conroy, who are respectively known for reprising, and literally defining, the roles of Harley Quinn, Joker and Batman ever since the 1992 animated series. It is inarguable that their performance as the said characters was so iconic and definitive that to this day, the successors resort to imitating their irreplaceable predecessors.

[b] GAMEPLAY AND LEVEL DESIGN [/b]
The gameplay is that part of the game that keeps pulling me back to it. Simply put, it's diverse, versatile, innovative and downright addictive. The combat system and the satisfaction of countering the enemy's attacks while returning them with acrobatic critical blows was absolutely unrivaled at its time and I daresay set the bar for later games that followed. The extensive upgrade system and gadgets that allow for strategic and creative takedowns are also an absolute joy to play around with.
The enemy variety and the assignment of specific fighting methods to particular variants is also a delightful challenge that keeps your head-cogs turning even through the seemingly generic fist-fights.
The Riddler challenges and collectibles are a side-segment of the game that could actually take more time to beat than the main story mode. (That is of course in case like myself, you refrain from looking up guides and walkthroughs online and prefer to rely on your own cognitive abilities instead.) But that eventual relieving moment of satisfaction and confidence-induction when you finally manage to solve a perplexing riddle or find a way to reach the cleverly concealed trophy is truly worth the hassle.
There also exist some supplementary "secrets" to be discovered which even further accentuate the spectral ambience that permeates the virulent air of the wacko-infested islet.

[b] CONCLUSION [/b]
Conclusively, despite the simple plot and lower-poly character models, the game has maintained its once-revolutionary brilliance and still manages to cast the same bewitching spell that charmed its players 13 years ago.
Rocksteady’s first Batman simulator is not just your ordinary action superhero video game. It is an immersive experience that allows the player to truly capture the surreal sensation of gliding through a mystifying realm of madness under the cowl of Gotham’s greatest detective.
So whether you are yet to experience the game, or merely wish to reminisce the memories you made playing it, the title is definitely worth your purchase in 2023.

**SPOILER-FREE REVIEW**

[u]~Story~[/u]

As the first game of Batman Arkham series, Asylum succeeds in every way in my point of view. I will be honest from the start and confess that I played all these series in no particular order  leaving Asylum the last. You ask why? Well because compared to its successors I find that this game doesn't have too much of an unexpected plot. So yeah Batman finally caught Joker and he's bringing him to the Arkham Asylum, a place built on an island by Amadeus Arkham in hopes to cure the craziness in the villains of Gotham, to me even in comics this place resembles the prison Alcatraz due to it's location. In the Asylum Batman wishes to follow and take part in the incarceration of Joker mainly because he feels that something is wrong, our crazy clown would never let our caped vigilante catch him so easily and with new goons coming from Blackgate, we can say that B-man had his reasons. He was right, oh boy he was. So Joker frees himself while his inside "friends", Harley Quinn, take control over the whole building leaving the world's greatest detective fight goons and old powerful enemies who escaped in time after the outbreak while trying to get to the bottom of the case where Joker's true intentions on breaking the Asylum are discovered. Yes, the plot is exhilarating but I personally don't find it so unpredictable, still a very good narrative which I believed got an award and funny dialogues. Now that I think about it this game presents more humor than any other Arkham game. Many times I found myself laughing or grinning at Joker's stupid jokes and the interactions between characters.


[u]~Gameplay~[/u]

Gosh... Where to begin. The game is played from a third-person perspective, occasionally first-person in some cut-scenes or ventilation walking. It has a bit for everybody: stealth, parkour, fighting, crime scene scanning and following tracks, the whole game thrives in this category.  

As you are playing Batman you have at your disposal a variation of gadgets who you will unlock as you advance in the game but the first one you will have at the beginning will be the Batarang. I am sure you are all too familiar with this "ninja-star" like gadget use in disorienting enemies, stunning them, disabling stuff etc. The second one will have to be the Explosive Gel. It's basically what the name says, you spray it down on a weak surface and it goes K-Boom, helping you in taking down criminals and advance in the game. The third one and my favourite is the Bat Claw, initially the grapple that you use to climb on buildings or escape bad situations, after some progress you will be able to break down fragile walls, stun enemies bringing them to you and help you win the big boss fight. There are many others gadgets in the game, some unlocked only by upgrades but I find these the main and most iconic ones that will get you interested, others will help you open up gates, disable gas bombs, distract enemies etc.

Now let's talk about the combat. Batman Arkham has one of the best and satisfying combat systems ever made. Mainly involving 3 things: attacking, dodging/countering and stunning. But you can always spice it up using some gadgets. Compared with the other games in the series this one is more complicated in my opinion. The counter attacks are a bit late and work when work only with perfect timing while there is no knife escape and all these I found them annoying even tough it might not sound like a big deal. After experiencing this I clearly saw the foundation that the developers used in improving the game and combat, and creating the future masterpieces after this monumental achievement.

OK so we covered up the main stuff but I wanna talk about the upgrades who I remained fairly disappointed of how less they are, mainly consisting in armor upgrading and combos. The other ones are just gadgets.

Riddles. Oh riddles... I am ashamed to say that I never gathered all Enigma's trophies but that's probably because of my laziness because the Asylum is not a big map so for who is patient enough and has the ambition to find them all and solve all the riddles you will find yourselves succeeding in no time.


[u]~Graphics and Soundtrack~[/u]

This game's graphics are amazing and it was released in 2009. The graphics engine belongs to Unreal Engine 3 supporting DirectX 9, frame rate did not drop lower then 60 in my experience.  They all have a comic book 3D look about it which only makes them more suiting for this game. The team said that they used a series of saturated colors in order to transform the place  into a grim looking asylum, bleeding with desperation and insanity. The architecture presents a Gothic look and the sewers and underground structures resemble the Victorian industry. Everything is made to look over-the-top and extravagant and it brought me many times thinking about the comic itself and I confess that Arkham Asylum has the best design compared to the others even in the menu section and character's bios the comic look still stands strong. The originality struck me and I couldn't love it more. As for the details, I advice anybody who wants to enjoy this game at it's best, to use a good graphic card. The details that this place has are INSANE. To files that are scattered around showing familiar names to the smallest pictures on the ground. Jesus at the beginning I couldn't even believe that somebody would take his time for this but the effort was well used.

As for the music I absolutely loved it. Eerie, strange, Gothic instrumentals that created this amazing experience through out the game. Don't have much to say about it though just that it was fitting for this whole place.


[u]~Conclusion~[/u]

Batman Arkham Asylum is the daddy. The entire game was well created. It was creepy, funny, action paced, just a bit of everything and in good measures. The voice actors brought life to the characters, beautiful design helped immersing in this "wonderland" of insanity and the combat system and stealth approaches makes everything fun and challenging. A masterpiece of a game hands down.

This review is based on 100% completion and 23.3 hours of gameplay.

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Do I recommend this game? Yes, even though this is an old game, it is still really fun to play. While the controls and gameplay may feel clunky and unintuitive given its age, the game is still very well made. 

I bought this as part of the Batman: Arkham Collection and have yet to play the other games in it, but this game is a good buy; however, as always, waiting for a sale is the best option. 

If you want the best bang for your buck, I would wait until the bundle goes on sale before purchasing this.

[h1][b]Experience:[/b][/h1]
[b]Base game:[/b] This is a short and very good story; if you wanted to, you could finish it in one sitting in about 8 hours, going very slowly. 

It's interesting to see how the environment changes as the story progresses. In addition to Batman's wear and tear throughout the game, this is a nice little detail. It's also exciting to see some iconic characters appear throughout the story. 

The controls can feel clunky and unintuitive at times, but this is simply due to the game's age, as it was released in 2010. Despite the controls' clunkiness, they still feel good because they don't have hundreds of controls and buttons, unlike certain street fighter games.

[b]Challenge mode:[/b] I dislike challenge modes in all games, and this one is no exception. It plays exactly as expected, with the same gameplay as the base game, but in an arena setting, attempting to complete the challenges for each arena.  

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1] 
There is an amazing guide for this game created by [i][b]"Cynic 0055"[/b][/i] in the steam guides that goes over the collectables as you can get them with minimal backtracking, which is awesome to help cut down on the time needed to do the collectables, as well as showing when you can complete achievements during the story. 

This game has a lot of collectibles, so using the guide is recommended, but it is not required if you want the challenge; they are still very doable without the guide, it just takes longer. 

[b]Base game:[/b] The achievements in the base game can be completed in two runs if you want to take it easy, or in one if you want to play on the hardest difficulty right away. These are fairly simple; the majority are story-related and will unlock as you progress; others are miscellaneous and very easy to complete; and the collectables are simple if you follow the guide; otherwise, it will take longer. 

There are a few [b]missables[/b], so double-check before starting. 

[b]Challenge mode:[/b] These will be the most annoying of all the achievements in the game, especially the combat challenges, because the score is quite high and you will need to master the game's mechanics as well as a little luck because the controls are definitely not the best. Just the combat challenges took me about 1-2 hours, so they are doable; they are just very annoying. When it comes to the predator challenge achievements, they are easier, and if you're having trouble, there are videos online that can help these took around 30 minutes to an hour.  

Overall, the achievements are not too bad, but if you are like me and are bad at fighting games, some of them may be a little annoying.

[h1]Fantastically satisfying & well-designed // Recommended even for those who don't care for the Batman franchise[/h1]

+ Voice-acting is spectacular; dialogue stays true to the lore, and lines are competently delivered (with the notable exception being Gordon's character)
+ Combat system is simple, fluid and enjoyable; attacks are well-rendered, feel as though they have weight to them, and offer the player an opportunity for great finesse
+ Detective mode is an excellent mechanic, and adds significantly to gameplay
+ Myriad unlockables and collectibles scattered throughout; character bios, therapy audio files, riddler trophies, etc. are all fun to collect and do well to showcase the lore of the franchise
+ Mechanics are refreshingly varied and intuitively introduced; the way that Batman's utilities work to influence the environment is applaudable in its implementation
+ Devs showed great care in the nuances of design; Batman's suit shows gradual accumulation of wear and damage, and his beard shows visible signs of growth as the story progresses
+ Platforming mechanics are near perfect, and the game does much to encourage their utilization; problems can often be tackled in many different ways depending on how the environment is utilized
+ Audio design is superb
+ Boss fights require a healthy balance of reflex and making on-the-spot decisions
+ Environmental detail is excellent; the devs clearly took great care in modelling the island, and the quality really comes through in the final product
+ Game's engine runs smoothly and efficiently

- Facial animations are atrocious
- Abysmal variation in enemy mob design; game relies heavily on a copy/paste approach
- Very poor variety in voiceovers for secondary characters and enemy mobs; it seems as though all support characters are voiced by 3 or 4 individuals
- Textures have not aged well, and contrast sharply with quality in lighting
- Standard enemy mobs have one, solitary KO animation; this animation is used uniformly throughout the entire game, and it is a decidedly ugly one at that

Batman Arkham Asylum still holds up incredibly well, especially for a game from 2009. The combat system is smooth, satisfying, and makes you feel like Batman without being overly complicated. I was also surprised by how good the graphics and overall presentation still look today.

What stood out to me most was the atmosphere of Arkham Asylum itself. The game really captures the dark Batman feeling, and exploring the asylum made the world feel memorable rather than just like a simple action game. I also enjoyed the Riddler challenges because they gave me a reason to explore more carefully and pay attention to the details.

Overall, I enjoyed the entire experience. It has great combat, strong atmosphere, fun side challenges, and it is easy to see why this game is still considered one of the best superhero games. I would definitely recommend it to Batman fans and action-adventure players.
